sections.title: 1.1 · Convolutions from scratch
paragraphs: Convolution flips the kernel in both dimensions and sums the products of overlapping samples. Both implementations use zero padding outside the image. The four-loop implementation iterates over image rows, image columns, kernel rows, and kernel columns. The two-loop implementation keeps the two kernel loops and operates on a complete shifted image slice at each step. Neither implementation uses a convolution routine, FFT, window-view helper, or image-processing library.

For a kernel of height Kh and width Kw, let K denote the kernel size along one axis. The padding is floor(K/2) samples before that axis and floor((K−1)/2) after it. For even kernels, this asymmetry matches SciPy’s “same” output convention. Comparisons use non-symmetric odd and even kernels because a symmetric Gaussian alone cannot reveal a reversed kernel or a one-pixel offset.

The self portrait is converted to grayscale using 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B, with RGB values in [0, 1]. The working image is 384 × 512 pixels. A normalized 9 × 9 box filter and the derivative kernels Dₓ and Dᵧ are applied separately.

The box filter removes fine texture. Dₓ and Dᵧ emphasize changes across columns and rows, respectively; their signed responses share a symmetric color scale. Zero padding darkens the outer rim of the smoothed image and can produce derivative responses at the frame.

The runtime comparison uses a fixed 96 × 96 image resized from the self portrait. Each method uses float64 values, zero padding, and “same” output. The table reports the median of three calls after one warm-up, with a maximum absolute error of 8.88e-16 across all comparisons.

For an H × W image and a Kh × Kw kernel, both manual methods require O(HWKhKw) arithmetic. Operating on image slices removes Python’s per-pixel loop overhead. The reported times describe performance on this computer.

The boundary comparison uses a constant 25 × 25 image with value one and a normalized 9 × 9 box filter. Zero padding gives 25/81 at a corner and 5/9 at the midpoint of an edge; symmetric and periodic extension preserve one everywhere. The “same” setting controls output size, while the boundary setting supplies values outside the image.

code.title: Input validation, kernel reversal, and padding
code.text:
def _convolution_inputs(image, kernel):
    image = np.asarray(image, dtype=np.float64)
    kernel = np.asarray(kernel, dtype=np.float64)
    if image.ndim != 2 or kernel.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("image and kernel must both be two dimensional")
    if not image.size or not kernel.size:
        raise ValueError("image and kernel must be nonempty")
    kh, kw = kernel.shape
    # Before = ceil((K-1)/2); after = floor((K-1)/2).
    padded = np.pad(image, ((kh // 2, (kh - 1) // 2),
                            (kw // 2, (kw - 1) // 2)), mode='constant')
    return image, kernel[::-1, ::-1], padded

sections.title: 1.2 · Finite difference operator
paragraphs: Let I be the grayscale image. Its horizontal and vertical derivative responses are gx = I ∗ [1, 0, −1] and gy = I ∗ [1, 0, −1]ᵀ, where ∗ denotes convolution. Reversing the kernel during convolution makes a left-to-right increase in intensity produce positive gx. The gradient magnitude, √(gx² + gy²), combines the two responses into an unsigned measure of edge strength.

The supplied cameraman image has a thin white border. The crop (1, 7, 535, 541), given as (left, top, right, bottom) with the right and bottom coordinates excluded, removes that border. The remaining square is resized to 256 × 256 pixels with Lanczos interpolation. Calculations use floating-point intensities in [0, 1] without further normalization before thresholding.

A pixel is classified as an edge when its gradient magnitude exceeds the threshold T. A seven-pixel frame is excluded from binary maps and edge-fraction measurements throughout Part 1. This margin excludes responses caused by zero padding and covers the largest Gaussian derivative support used below. The signed derivative and magnitude images show the complete responses.

Thresholds of 0.08, 0.16, and 0.24 retain 23.7%, 12.8%, and 9.0% of the evaluated interior, respectively. The selected threshold, 0.16, preserves the person, camera, and tripod more clearly than 0.24 while rejecting much of the ground texture retained at 0.08. Selection is based on this visual balance; detection accuracy is not measured against annotated edges.

sections.title: 1.3 · Derivative of Gaussian
paragraphs: A 13 × 13 Gaussian kernel G with σ = 2 pixels is formed from the outer product of cv2.getGaussianKernel(13, 2) with itself. The image is first smoothed with G, then differentiated with Dₓ and Dᵧ.

Alternatively, Kx = G ∗ Dₓ and Ky = G ∗ Dᵧ combine smoothing and differentiation into one image convolution per direction. These finite-difference derivatives of the sampled Gaussian have supports of 13 × 15 and 15 × 13 pixels because full kernel convolution retains the extra two samples.

Convolution associativity gives I ∗ (G ∗ D) = (I ∗ G) ∗ D for an image extended with zeros. Applying “same” output after each stage crops the intermediate blurred image and removes values beyond the original frame. These removed values affect the subsequent derivative near the boundary.

The two successive “same” convolutions differ from a single Gaussian derivative convolution by at most 0.307 over the complete image, while the evaluated interior agrees to 8.95e-16. Retaining the full blurred image, applying the derivative, and cropping once reduces the maximum difference to 8.95e-16. The difference images show where the intermediate crop affects the result.

The derivative of Gaussian (DoG) suppresses fine grass texture and produces smoother, wider contours than finite differences on the original image. Smoothing can also merge nearby edges and remove weak detail. The selected thresholds are T = 0.08 for DoG and T = 0.16 for the original gradients because smoothing reduces response amplitudes. These thresholds support a visual comparison at separately chosen settings; they do not establish a difference in detection accuracy.

The noise experiment adds Gaussian noise with σ = 0.08 using a fixed random seed, then clips intensities to [0, 1]. Each noisy gradient is compared with the same method applied to the clean image. This comparison measures the change caused by noise while retaining each method’s smoothing effect.

The root mean square (RMS) of the interior vector-gradient residual decreases from 0.15226 for finite differences to 0.01030 for DoG, a factor of 14.8. Gaussian smoothing therefore reduces sensitivity to the added noise in this experiment. The measurement describes this image and noise realization; it does not measure recovery of detail removed by smoothing.

sections.title: Gradient orientations
paragraphs: Gradient orientation uses the Gaussian-derivative responses gx and gy from Section 1.3. The calculation uses arithmetic operations without calling an arctangent, atan2, or angle routine. For nonzero gradients, r = min(|gy|, |gx|)/max(|gy|, |gx|) lies between zero and one. For r > √2−1, the identity atan(r) = π/4 + atan((r−1)/(r+1)) reduces the magnitude of the series argument to at most √2−1.

The arctangent is approximated with 18 terms of z − z³/3 + z⁵/5 − …, where z is the reduced argument. Coordinate swaps and the signs of the gradient components determine the quadrant. A zero gradient is assigned orientation zero and displayed black.

The HSV display maps orientation θ to hue (θ mod 2π)/(2π), with saturation one. Brightness is min(magnitude / p99.5, 1)^0.7, where p99.5 = 0.2386 is the 99.5th percentile of gradient magnitude in the evaluated interior. Stronger gradients appear brighter, while weak background responses remain subdued. The seven-pixel boundary margin is displayed black.

Color indicates the direction of increasing intensity, perpendicular to the edge tangent. Image rows increase downward, so 90° points down. Comparison with NumPy atan2, used only for validation, gives a maximum angular error of 4.44e-16 radians for this image.

figures.caption: Gradient orientation and direction color wheel. Hue represents direction in image coordinates; brightness represents edge strength. The seven-pixel boundary margin is excluded.
figures.alt: Gradient orientation and direction color wheel. Hue represents direction in image coordinates; brightness represents edge strength. The seven-pixel boundary margin is excluded.

code.title: Arithmetic-only orientation implementation
code.text:
def orientation_without_angles(gx, gy, terms=18):
    """Quadrant-correct atan2 equivalent using arithmetic and a Taylor series.

    No arctan/arctan2/angle function is used. Range reduction first replaces
    the ratio by min(|y|,|x|)/max(|y|,|x|), then uses
      atan(r) = pi/4 + atan((r-1)/(r+1)) for r > tan(pi/8).
    This bounds the series argument by sqrt(2)-1, giving fast convergence.
    At a zero gradient the angle is assigned zero (orientation is undefined).
    Signed-zero distinctions on the negative x-axis are immaterial for hue.
    """
    gx, gy = np.broadcast_arrays(np.asarray(gx, float), np.asarray(gy, float))
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(gx)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(gy)):
        raise ValueError('gradient components must be finite')
    if terms < 1:
        raise ValueError('terms must be positive')
    ax, ay = np.abs(gx), np.abs(gy)
    high, low = np.maximum(ax, ay), np.minimum(ax, ay)
    ratio = np.divide(low, high, out=np.zeros_like(high), where=high != 0)
    reduce = ratio > np.sqrt(2.0) - 1.0
    z = np.where(reduce, (ratio - 1.0) / (ratio + 1.0), ratio)
    # Horner evaluation of z - z^3/3 + z^5/5 - ... .
    z2 = z * z
    poly = np.zeros_like(z)
    for n in range(terms - 1, -1, -1):
        poly = ((-1.0) ** n) / (2 * n + 1) + z2 * poly
    small_angle = z * poly + np.where(reduce, np.pi / 4, 0.0)
    angle = np.where(ay > ax, np.pi / 2 - small_angle, small_angle)
    angle = np.where(gx < 0, np.pi - angle, angle)
    angle = np.where(gy < 0, -angle, angle)
    return np.where(high == 0, 0.0, angle)

sections.title: 2.1 · Image sharpening
paragraphs: For an input image I and Gaussian kernel G, let B = G ∗ I be the low-pass image and H = I − B its high-frequency residual. Unsharp masking adds a scaled residual: S = I + αH, where α controls the sharpening amount.

Expanding the residual gives S = (1 + α)I − α(G ∗ I). The equivalent convolution kernel is K = (1 + α)δ − αG, where δ is the unit impulse, so S = K ∗ I requires one convolution. K sums to one and preserves a constant image when the boundary extension also preserves constants.

The experiment uses a 13 × 13 Gaussian with σ = 2 pixels and symmetric boundary extension. Each RGB channel is processed independently in float64, retaining signed residuals and values outside [0, 1] until display export. Symmetric extension avoids the dark borders introduced by zero padding. The Taj Mahal and an original street photograph are processed at α = 0.5, 1, and 2.

Increasing α strengthens existing edges and texture, but also amplifies noise and halos and increases values outside the display range. Residuals are displayed as 0.5 + 2H, with middle gray representing zero and a fixed amplification of two. No independent normalization is applied to these residuals. The table reports the fraction of scalar RGB values outside [0, 1] before display clipping.

The single-convolution result agrees with S = I + α(I − G ∗ I) at α = 1 to a maximum absolute error of 1.78e-15 across the two images. This comparison checks the equivalence of the residual and kernel formulations.

The recovery experiment first blurs the original street image, then sharpens that blurred image with the same Gaussian at each tested α. Mean squared error (MSE) is measured over RGB values relative to the original image, both before and after display clipping. For the reference range [0, 1], peak signal-to-noise ratio is PSNR = 10 log10(1/MSE), in decibels.

Among the tested settings, α = 2 gives the lowest clipped RGB MSE. The MSE changes from 0.001660 after blurring to 0.001099 after sharpening, while PSNR changes from 27.80 to 29.59 dB. This parameter is selected against the original reference and applies to this comparison.

Sharpening makes blurred transitions steeper but leaves differences from the original image. If G(f) is the Gaussian frequency response, the combined blur and sharpening response is G(f)[1 + α − αG(f)], which generally differs from one. Frequencies strongly attenuated by the blur remain attenuated after this finite amplification, and clipping can remove additional information. The enlarged crop, residual map, and nonzero MSE show that increased edge contrast does not restore all original detail.

sections.title: 2.2 · Hybrid images
paragraphs: A hybrid image combines a blurred image with fine detail from a second, aligned image: hybrid = G_sigmaL * A + gain (B - G_sigmaH * B). G_sigma is a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation sigma, and * denotes convolution. A supplies broad structure and B supplies fine detail. The examples are Derek + Nutmeg, astronaut + portrait cat, and Obama + Einstein.

For the portrait-cat pairs, the initial alignment maps both pairs of eye centers to (170,210) and (330,210). Each two-point similarity transform combines rotation, uniform scale and translation. Exact eye alignment leaves a separate human mouth or chin below the cat muzzle. The broad smile remains in the low-frequency component, so increasing fur contrast alone does not remove it.

For Derek and the astronaut, the human portrait is scaled by 0.70 about (250,210), while the cat remains fixed. Derek is also shifted upward by 12 pixels. This places the lower human face within the cat muzzle, at the cost of coincident eye landmarks. Obama and Einstein instead share eye targets (196,205) and (316,205); no separate geometry refinement is used. The geometry table records the low-source transforms relative to each pair’s common eye alignment.

Each original is resampled once with the composed similarity transform, using bilinear interpolation and replicated borders. The face proportions are unchanged. The original landmarks and exact 2 x 3 transformation matrices are saved with the experiment records.

The selected high-pass widths, 1.5 pixels for the portrait-cat pairs and 2.5 pixels for Obama + Einstein, suppress broader source structure than sigma 5. Less of that structure remains in reduced views. The selected (low-pass sigma, high-pass sigma, gain) settings are Derek + Nutmeg: (8, 1.5, 2.25); Astronaut + portrait cat: (10, 1.5, 2.7); Obama + Einstein: (12, 2.5, 2). Larger low-pass widths soften the teeth and chin while retaining broad facial structure.

The six filter-width and gain trials keep the selected alignment fixed. Increasing the astronaut low-pass sigma to 18 blurs the eyes and smile in the reduced view. Increasing its high-pass sigma from 1.5 to 3 retains broader cat structure, which competes with the human face. The controlled comparisons vary alignment and filtering separately. These settings are selected visually for these particular inputs.

Reducing human scale and smoothing the low-frequency source suppress the separate lower mouth and chin contour in the near view. Cat eyes and muzzle dominate at 512 and 256 pixels. The astronaut remains recognizable at 64 pixels; the 128-pixel view is mixed.

On refined geometry, changing from reference to selected filters changes clipping from 3.86% to 2.69%. With selected filters fixed, refining geometry changes clipping from 1.69% to 2.69%. The smaller human image reduces the separate lower mouth and chin, but displaces the eye landmarks. This is a visual tradeoff, not evidence of more accurate landmark registration. Intermediate views remain mixed.

To inspect the effect, view the largest image at normal size and then move farther away, keeping its display size fixed. The reduced versions provide a second comparison. The apparent change depends on screen size, zoom and eyesight, so the pixel-size sequence does not establish a calibrated viewing distance.

A Gaussian has no sharp frequency cutoff. Its approximate half-amplitude frequency is sqrt(2 ln 2) / (2 pi sigma) cycles per output pixel. For the selected astronaut pair, this is 0.0187 for the low pass and 0.1249 for the complementary high pass. Filtering uses spatial convolution; the Fourier plots show the resulting frequency content.

Each Fourier spectrum displays log(1 + 1000000 |fftshift(fft2(luminance))| / N), where N is the number of image pixels. Division by N permits comparison of differently sized inputs, and both figures use one shared display maximum. No window or mean subtraction is applied before the Fourier transform.

Filtering uses reflected boundaries, and filtering and addition retain signed float64 values. Intermediate bands are neither clipped nor contrast-normalized. Display exports clamp values to [0,1] and quantize them to 8 bits; the table reports the fraction of scalar channel values clipped. Supplementary figures include the remaining alignment, component and parameter comparisons, together with the unsuccessful Earth + Moon hybrid.

sections.title: Color in hybrid images
paragraphs: Four variants retain color in neither source, only the low-frequency source, only the high-frequency source, or both. Color in the low-frequency source preserves the astronaut’s broad skin and hair regions. Color in the high-frequency source appears around fine cat edges, but the filtering removes the broad coat color.

For this pair, color in the low-frequency source agrees with the face visible at smaller sizes, while grayscale fur remains visible at larger sizes. Retaining color in both sources adds competing hues around some cat edges. The main examples use grayscale so that the change in visible subject can be assessed without this broad color difference.

figures.caption: Four color variants with identical alignment, filter widths and gain. Luminance conversion uses weights 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722. Color in the low-frequency source preserves broad skin and hair regions; color in the high-frequency source remains mainly around cat edges and fur.

sections.title: 2.3 · Gaussian and Laplacian stacks
paragraphs: The supplied apple and orange images are burt_apple.png and burt_orange.png. Each 740 × 530 input is resized once to a common working size of 512 × 367 pixels using area interpolation. This reduces the computational cost while preserving the original aspect ratio to the nearest output pixel.

A Gaussian stack retains the same image dimensions at every level. G0 = I is the original image; G1 through G5 are formed by independently blurring I at σ = 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 pixels. Each σ therefore describes the smoothing relative to the original image. The stack is constructed explicitly without downsampling or a built-in pyramid routine.

The Laplacian detail bands are Li = Gi − G(i+1) for i = 0, …, 4, and L5 = G5 is the coarse residual. Summing the detail bands gives I − G5; including the residual restores the large-scale brightness and color. The complete sum reconstructs I up to floating-point rounding. The table reports the reconstruction error for each input and for the blended image.

A binary mask selects apple on the left and orange on the right. Its Gaussian stack uses the same smoothing scales as the image stacks. At level i, Mi is the mask and LAi and LBi are the apple and orange Laplacian bands; the combined band is Si = Mi LAi + (1 − Mi) LBi. This expression also applies to the coarse residual, and summing all Si gives the final image.

The mask has a sharp transition at the finest level and progressively wider transitions at coarser levels. Fine texture and broad changes in brightness and color are therefore blended over different spatial ranges. The contribution figure shows selected detail levels and the complete reconstruction.

figures.caption: Apple: Gaussian stack above and Laplacian stack below, including the coarse residual. Every level retains the working resolution of 512 × 367 pixels. Signed detail bands use 0.5 + 2.5L for display; the residual uses its actual intensity.

Orange: Gaussian stack above and Laplacian stack below, including the coarse residual. Every level retains the working resolution of 512 × 367 pixels. Signed detail bands use 0.5 + 2.5L for display; the residual uses its actual intensity.
Gaussian stack of the left/right selection mask, using the same scales as the image stacks. The transition widens at coarser levels. White selects apple and black selects orange.

Figure 3.42 (a)–(l) layout: rows 1–3 show levels 0, 2, and 4; columns show the masked apple, masked orange, and their sum. Row 4 sums all five detail bands and the coarse residual to reconstruct the two contributions and final oraple. Detail bands share a symmetric display scale within each row; reconstructed images use actual [0, 1] intensity.

code.text:
G = [I] + [gaussian(I, 2 * 2**i) for i in range(5)]
L = [G[i] - G[i+1] for i in range(5)] + [G[-1]]
S = [M[i] * LA[i] + (1-M[i]) * LB[i] for i in range(6)]
result = sum(S)

sections.title: 2.4 · Multiresolution blending
paragraphs: The apple and orange are combined using the same inputs and initial selection mask for both methods. A direct binary cut produces a visible vertical change in brightness and color. Multiresolution blending combines corresponding Laplacian bands with Gaussian mask weights, spreading the transition according to scale while retaining local texture.

The mean absolute RGB difference between the columns adjoining the seam decreases from 0.1716 for the binary cut to 0.0279 for the multiresolution blend. This local measurement is consistent with the smoother visible transition. It describes the seam discontinuity rather than overall perceptual quality.

The seam measurement uses the floating-point reconstruction before clipping. Values remain unclipped throughout stack construction and reconstruction, then are limited to [0, 1] for display export. This affects 2.35% of scalar RGB values.

figures.caption: Supplied inputs, selection mask, direct binary cut, and multiresolution oraple. Both methods use the same 512 × 367 images with preserved aspect ratio. The seam lies between zero-based columns 255 and 256.

sections.title: Custom blends with irregular masks
paragraphs: The mountain-sky composite places Mount Rainier below a pink cloud field photographed above Denali. A 38-vertex polygon follows the visible cloud and mountain silhouette. It retains Rainier’s summit, glacier, foreground trees and the bright cloud on the left.

The Earth-Moon composite joins oceans and clouds to lunar craters along an S-shaped boundary. Their similar outlines support this composite, although the same photographs do not produce a clear change of subject in the hybrid experiment.

The largest source contours above luminance 0.04 are fitted with cv2.fitEllipse and mapped affinely to a circle of radius 220 pixels centered at (256,256). The Earth mapping uses axis scale factors differing by approximately 1%; the Moon mapping is nearly uniform.

The landscape photographs are independently cropped and uniformly scaled using saved framing points. These points set the output field of view; they are not corresponding features of the same scene. Both examples sample the original photographs with bilinear interpolation and replicated borders. Thresholding measures the planetary outlines only. Exposure and color are unchanged, and no retouching or prior background transfer precedes blending.

The hard cut, single-scale feathering and multiresolution blend use identical input arrays and the same underlying binary selection. Feathering applies the exact coarsest Gaussian mask to the full images, so fine details and broad colors mix over the same wide transition. Multiresolution blending applies the corresponding Gaussian mask to each Laplacian band.

A binary finest mask leaves visible polygon corners at the landscape boundary and a contrast change where the planetary boundary meets the outer edge. Initial-mask Gaussian widths of 0, 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 pixels are compared for each example. Landscape widths of 0, 2 and 4 give similar results; sigma 2 softens corners while preserving the summit outline. Earth-Moon uses sigma 8 to soften the outer-edge join.

Only the selection weights change; the source photographs and image detail bands remain fixed. Further smoothing at stack width sigma gives a nominal combined width of sqrt(initial_sigma² + sigma²). The landscape mask widths are 2, 2.8, 4.5, 8.2, 16.1 and 32.1 pixels. Earth-Moon uses 8, 8.2, 8.9, 11.3, 17.9, 33.0 and 64.5 pixels. The oraple retains a binary finest mask.

The landscape uses five detail bands with sigma = 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 pixels. The Earth-Moon blend uses six, adding sigma = 64 pixels, and both include the coarse residual. Supplementary comparisons test four, five and six bands while keeping all other inputs fixed.

For the landscape, the band-count differences are modest. A maximum sigma of 16 pixels leaves a narrower color transition. Sigma 32 spreads this transition locally; sigma 64 transfers more of the pink cast over the snow. The Earth-Moon blend uses sigma 64 because the brightness mismatch extends across a large part of the disk.

The landscape hard cut exposes the polygon above the summit and left cloud. Broad feathering mixes cloud texture through the ridge and makes the summit partly transparent. Multiresolution blending retains more local rock and snow contrast while spreading the broad sky-color transition. Some original cloud cover remains around the summit. Clouds and craters also remain more localized at the Earth-Moon boundary. These observations concern the visible transitions in these two examples.

The boundary-jump measurement is the mean absolute RGB difference between adjacent pixels on opposite sides of the original binary contour. It includes natural image texture as well as the seam. Feathering mixes detail across one broad transition; a smaller jump alone does not establish a better-looking or physically realistic composite.

RGB is used for the final composites. Pink clouds and orange-green foreground trees give the mountain-sky example stronger regional color differences. Blue oceans distinguish Earth from the nearly neutral Moon. These differences are less distinct in grayscale, although the boundaries remain smoothed.

Multiresolution blending does not correct scene geometry or illumination. The landscape combines different places and retains different lighting in the original and added clouds. It is not a photograph of a real scene. Lunar features likewise do not continue Earth’s clouds. Smoothing the finest mask reduces the abrupt outer-edge join, but the Earth-Moon composite remains an imaginary surface.
Processing retains signed float64 values. Only the final display images are clipped to [0,1].

hybrids.title: Derek + Nutmeg
hybrids.selection_note: The smaller human scale brings the lower face into the cat muzzle and reduces the separate chin contour. Nutmeg dominates the 512-pixel view; Derek becomes recognizable at 64 pixels. The 128-pixel view retains features from both sources.
hybrids.alignment_note: Relative to the common eye alignment, a global similarity transform scales the human image by 0.7 about (250,210) and translates it vertically by -12 pixels. The human eye centers map to [[194, 198], [306, 198]]; cat eye centers remain at (170,210) and (330,210). Each original is sampled once using the composed transform. This places the human mouth nearer the cat muzzle at the cost of exact eye coincidence; facial proportions are unchanged.

band_contrast_diagnostic.definition: std(high luminance) / std(low luminance); signed float Lanczos reduction, no clipping. Not a perceptual score.

hybrids.title: Astronaut + portrait cat
hybrids.selection_note: Reducing human scale and smoothing the low-frequency source suppress the separate lower mouth and chin contour in the near view. Cat eyes and muzzle dominate at 512 and 256 pixels. The astronaut remains recognizable at 64 pixels; the 128-pixel view is mixed.
hybrids.alignment_note: Relative to the common eye alignment, a global similarity transform scales the human image by 0.7 about (250,210) and translates it vertically by 0 pixels. The human eye centers map to [[194, 210], [306, 210]]; cat eye centers remain at (170,210) and (330,210). Each original is sampled once using the composed transform. This places the human mouth nearer the cat muzzle at the cost of exact eye coincidence; facial proportions are unchanged.

band_contrast_diagnostic.definition: std(high luminance) / std(low luminance); signed float Lanczos reduction, no clipping. Not a perceptual score.

hybrids.title: Obama + Einstein
hybrids.selection_note: Einstein’s hair, wrinkles and moustache dominate the 512-pixel view, while Obama’s broader facial structure and smile become clearer at 64 pixels. The 128-pixel view remains mixed. Sigma low 12 softens the broad smile patch without removing the low-frequency face; sigma high 2.5 and gain 2 preserve recognizable Einstein details while allowing these details to weaken on reduction. The near view retains an embossed appearance and faint low-frequency facial shading.
hybrids.alignment_note: Two-point similarity transforms map the eye centers in both originals to (196,205) and (316,205) on a 512 by 512 canvas. Uniform scaling, rotation and translation preserve facial proportions. The common eye targets are sufficient for this face-to-face pair; no local feature editing or separate geometry refinement is used.

band_contrast_diagnostic.definition: std(high luminance) / std(low luminance); signed float Lanczos reduction, no clipping. Not a perceptual score.

hybrids.title: Earth + Moon (limitation study)
hybrids.selection_note: The similar circular outlines and overlapping surface structure produce a textured planetary disk at both viewing scales. The result does not show a clear change in perceived subject.

band_contrast_diagnostic.definition: std(high luminance) / std(low luminance); signed float Lanczos reduction, no clipping. Not a perceptual score.

definitions.numerical_domain: Signed float64 image arrays before clipping, quantization, or JPEG export. Input RGB is scaled to [0,1]. JSON values are not rounded.
definitions.clip_fraction: Count of scalar RGB channel values strictly below 0 or above 1 divided by the total number of scalar RGB values.
definitions.clip_fraction_tolerance_1e6: Only the audit blending comparison additionally uses C_epsilon = mean(image < -1e-6 or image > 1+1e-6) over scalar RGB values, with epsilon = 1e-6. This tolerance discounts numerical roundoff and negligible excursions near display limits. The original strict clip_fraction and signed ranges are retained for every method; image computation and display export are unchanged. This is not a visual-quality score.
definitions.band_contrast_ratio: Population std(high luminance) / max(population std(low luminance), 1e-12), where high includes synthesis gain and luminance = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. Reuses hybrid_report._band_ratio: native 512-pixel bands are measured directly; 128-pixel bands use PIL signed float32 Lanczos reduction then float64 standard deviation. No clipping or uint8 conversion. This is a band-contrast diagnostic, not a perceptual or identity score.
definitions.boundary_jump: J = mean absolute RGB difference across all horizontal and vertical adjacent pixel pairs straddling the ORIGINAL binary selection contour, pooled equally over all pairs and channels. Reuses blend_report.boundary_jump. Natural image texture contributes; this is not an overall perceptual quality score.
definitions.feather: The exact coarsest Gaussian mask returned by multiresolution_blend weights the full registered sources: M_last A + (1-M_last) B. This is the same mask used for the multiscale coarse residual, including any configured initial mask smoothing.
definitions.rms: sqrt(mean(X**2)) over all pixels and RGB channels, with no centering, clipping, or contrast normalization.
definitions.mixed_contribution: S_i = M_i L_Ai + (1-M_i) L_Bi; L_i = G_i-G_(i+1) for detail levels, and L_5 = G_5 for the oraple coarse residual.
definitions.coarse_to_fine_trace: T_5 = S_5; T_k = T_(k+1) + S_k for k = 4,...,0. Remaining RMS is RMS(final-T_k), using the unmodified multiresolution_blend final. It need not decrease monotonically because signed bands can cancel. The endpoint can differ at floating-point roundoff because the accumulation order differs.
definitions.fine_to_coarse_trace: U_i = sum(S_0,...,S_i); remaining RMS = RMS(final-U_i). Retained as a numerical cross-check, not the primary report trace.
definitions.saved_checks: Numeric matches use numpy.allclose with rtol=1e-12 and atol=1e-12 against results/frequencies.json; configuration labels and landmarks must match exactly. A mismatch raises AssertionError.
definitions.interpretation: No reference composite or ground truth is available. These diagnostics do not establish MSE, SSIM, perceptual quality, or a calibrated viewing distance.
